While he was shouting, she was typing and saying nothing.

It was raining when we arrived at the hotel.
There was a line of people at the desk, and nobody was moving.
While we were waiting, the hotel told us it was overbooked.
As soon as I asked what they could do for us, everything changed.
Eventually they sorted it out, and it turned out fine.

People think a hotel overbooks by accident. It does not. We sell more rooms than we have because on a normal night four or five guests never turn up, and an empty room earns nothing. Nine nights out of ten the arithmetic works and nobody notices. On the tenth night everybody turns up, and I am the one standing at that desk. Here is what I was taught on my first shift, and I still do it. I tell the guest the truth in the first sentence, before they ask, because the anger comes from not knowing. Then I say what I am going to do, not what I cannot do. We pay for the room in the other hotel, we pay for the taxi, and we bring the guest back the next morning at no cost. And I have learned one more thing in eleven years. The guests who make a big noise do not get more than the guests who stay calm and ask a clear question. They only get it later, because while they are shouting, nobody is typing.

So this happened to me in Lisbon two years ago, and I still tell the story. We landed at eleven at night, it was raining, and when we got to the hotel there was a line of about nine people at the desk. Nobody was moving. While we were waiting, I heard the man in front of us shouting at the receptionist about a booking he had made in March. He shouted for ten minutes and he got nothing. When it was our turn, my wife did something very simple. She put the reservation on the counter, she smiled, and she asked one question: what can you do for us tonight? The receptionist typed for about forty seconds, and then she gave us a room in a better hotel two streets away, a taxi and breakfast. As soon as we walked out, the man was still at the desk, still shouting. It turned out he stayed there another hour.
